"First things first" means: do the most important thing before anything else.

It is a reminder — to yourself or to others — that priorities matter. Before you jump into less important tasks, you must handle the most critical one first.

Think of it this way: if your house is on fire, you don't stop to water your plants before calling the fire department. You deal with the fire first, because that is the most urgent and important thing. That mindset is exactly what this idiom captures.

The phrase is almost self-explanatory once you look at it carefully:

  • "First things" = the most important things, the top priorities
  • "First" (at the end) = before other things, ahead of everything else

So when you put it together: "The most important things should come before the less important things."

This idiom is used in two main ways:

1. As a reminder to yourself
When you feel overwhelmed or scattered, you might say it to refocus your mind on what truly matters right now.

"I have a hundred things to do today. First things first — I need to finish this report before the deadline."

2. To redirect or guide someone else
You can say it to someone who is getting distracted or jumping ahead.

"I know you're excited about the party decorations, but first things first — have you sent out the invitations yet?"

In both cases, the idiom gently but firmly says: stop, slow down, and think about what deserves your attention right now.

This idiom carries a sense of discipline, wisdom, and common sense. It is not urgent or panicked. It is calm and logical. When someone says "first things first," they are being organized and thoughtful. They are saying: "Let's not get ahead of ourselves. Let's handle what matters most, in the right order."

Here are some real-life situations where this idiom fits naturally:

  • A student has exams tomorrow but wants to play video games. A parent says: "First things first — study for your exam. You can play later."
  • Someone wants to plan a road trip but hasn't saved any money yet. A friend says: "First things first — build up your savings. The trip can wait."
  • A new employee is excited about leading big projects on their first day. A mentor says: "First things first — learn how the company works before taking on leadership."
  • You wake up late and have a meeting in an hour. You think: "First things first — I need to get dressed and leave the house. Breakfast can wait."

The phrase has been around for a long time. It is widely believed to trace back to the late 1800s. One of the most famous early uses is credited to George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright and author, who reportedly said:

"The secret to success is to know what has to be done first."

The more direct version — "first things first" — became popular as a practical life motto, especially in self-improvement and organizational thinking. In the 20th century, it was famously used by Stephen Covey, the author of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, as one of his core habits — dedicating an entire chapter and later a whole book to the idea that prioritizing the right things is the key to a productive and meaningful life.

Over time, the phrase moved from formal writing into everyday speech, and today it is used casually by people all over the world.

This idiom is neutral and versatile — it works in almost every situation:

  • In casual conversation with friends and family ✓
  • In professional settings like meetings or workplaces ✓
  • In personal self-talk when organizing your thoughts ✓
  • In writing, both informal and semi-formal ✓

It is never rude or offensive. At most, it can sound slightly firm or authoritative when used to redirect someone — but in a helpful, not harsh, way.

To understand an idiom fully, it helps to know what it does not mean:

  • It does not mean "do everything quickly."
  • It does not mean "ignore everything except the top task forever."
  • It does not mean "be selfish and put yourself first."

It simply means: in this moment, identify the most important step and take that step before moving on to other things.

These phrases carry a related meaning and are good to know alongside this idiom:

  • "One step at a time" — focus on each stage in order, don't rush ahead.
  • "Don't put the cart before the horse" — don't do things in the wrong order.
  • "Start from the beginning" — begin at the logical starting point.
  • "Prioritize" — more formal, but the same core idea.
A Simple Way to Remember It Forever

Picture a to-do list. Some tasks are starred ⭐ because they are urgent and important. Others can wait. "First things first" is the voice in your head that says: "Do the starred ones first. Everything else comes after."

That's it. That's the whole idiom. It is a simple, timeless reminder that order matters, and important things deserve to come first.
